source_text: CAPUT OCTAVUM, Demonstratur, resurrectionem carnis a nonnullis, quibus de scripturae authoritate constat, negari. Resurrectio carnis a nonnullis qui sacrae scripturae authoritatem agnoscunt, perperam negatur, ab aliis vero & melioribus firmiter asseritur. II. Negatur vel ab antiquis, vel a quibusdam recentioribus. III. Ab antiquis, ut Sadduceis, Hymenaeo, Phileto & similibus.
english: CHAPTER EIGHT. It is demonstrated that the resurrection of the flesh is denied by some to whom the authority of Scripture is established.
The resurrection of the flesh is wrongly denied by some who acknowledge the authority of Sacred Scripture, but is firmly asserted by others and better ones.
II. It is denied either by the ancients or by certain more recent ones.
III. By the ancients, as by the Sadducees, Hymenaeus, Philetus, and the like.

source_text: Impudenter vero Farello insultat Franciscus Feuardentius ad Irenaeum lib. 5. c. 2. eumque scribit abire in castra Simonianorum & Marcionitarum, quod videatur ei resurrectio carnis in τῶν ἀδυνάτων, ex iis quae fieri nequeant. Probe enim noverat Farellus, quae impossibilia sunt apud homines, possibilia esse apud Deum, Luc. 18.27. cui non erit impossibile ullum verbum, Luc. 1.37. sed indicare duntaxat voluit, humano eam judicio impossibilem videri: quippe qui non simpliciter corporis, sed carnis hujus, qua nunc induimur, resurrectionem a nobis credi debere, epistola ad Calvinum scripta confertissimis & solidis argumentis probat, ut doctissimus Vossius thes. de resurr. docet. Sed clarissimus Rivetus synopsi purioris theol. disp. 51. th. 27. observat epistolam Calvini ad Laelium Socinum esse, quae falso inscripta sit Farellus Calvino, ob quam Feuardentius Calvino insultat.
english: But Franciscus Feuardentius shamelessly insults Farel on Irenaeus book 5, chapter 2, and writes that he goes off into the camps of the Simonians and Marcionites, because the resurrection of the flesh seems to him among the ἀδύνατα, among those things which cannot happen. For Farel well knew that things impossible with humans are possible with God (Luke 18:27), for whom no word will be impossible (Luke 1:37): but he wished only to indicate that by human judgment it seems impossible — inasmuch as he proves by a letter written to Calvin with most dense and solid arguments that not simply the resurrection of a body, but of this flesh with which we are now clothed, ought to be believed by us, as the most learned Vossius teaches in his thesis On the Resurrection. But the most clear Rivetus (Synopsis of Purer Theology, disputation 51, thesis 27) observes that it is Calvin's letter to Laelius Socinus, which was falsely titled Farel to Calvin, on account of which Feuardentius insults Calvin.

source_text: Si quaeratur, quomodo id intelligant, nempe inquiunt, ut homo sciat animam suam spiritum immortalem esse perpetuo viventem in caelis: ac Christum morte sua opinationem abolivisse, eaque ratione nobis restituisse vitam, quae in eo est, ut nos minime mori cognoscamus. Sed & nostri temporis Photiniani, Weigelianii & Rosaecrucii similesque fanatici hunc Valentini errorem recoquunt, & prae caeteris Chymici superstitiosiores, pedibus euntes in Theophrasti Paracelsi opiniones & teretismata quaedam, delusi analogismo quodam artis suae, e tribus veluti mundis, elementari videlicet angelico & divino, triplicia corpora, imo & animas & spiritus evocare audent, quibus catholica fides, tanquam sol meridianus, quo crepera & tenebrosa illorum sapientiae aurora cum templis & portis apertis cordium dissipatur, e myrotheciis sacrarum literarum cordate opponenda est.
english: If it be asked how they understand that, they say namely that a human may know that his soul is an immortal spirit perpetually living in the heavens; and that Christ by his death abolished the false opinion, and by that reason restored to us the life which is in him, so that we may know that we by no means die. But also the Photinians, Weigelians, and Rosicrucians of our time and like fanatics recook this error of Valentinus, and above the rest the more superstitious chemists, going on foot into Theophrastus Paracelsus's opinions and certain trifles, deceived by a certain analogy of their art, dare to evoke from three as it were worlds — namely elemental, angelic, and divine — threefold bodies, nay even souls and spirits: against whom the catholic faith is to be opposed courteously from the perfume-boxes of the sacred letters, as the midday sun by which the dusky and dark dawn of their wisdom is scattered with temples and open doors of hearts.

source_text: IV. Ex recentioribus Christi nomen professis, non ita quidem multi eo temeritatis ac profanitatis procedunt, ut resurrectionem carnis inficientur aperte: attamen non desunt, qui veteres haereses etiam in hac doctrinae parte interpolatas & incrustatas ab orco revocare non verecundantur. Imperatore Aenobarbi filio, Almaricus Parisiensis Doctor hunc errorem inter alios amplexus, Lutetiae cum sociis & sectatoribus exustus est. Johannes XXIII. Papa Romanus ut immortalitatem animae, sic & carnis resurrectionem negavit. De Libertinis patrum nostrorum memoria exortis, & multa cum Cerdone, Valentino & Marcione communia habentibus, magnus Johannes Calvinus Instructionis cap. 3. Quicquid, ait, Christiani de vita aeterna, de resurrectione tenent, ipsis fabula est. Hoc enim imaginantur, animam hominis, quae est Deus, ad seipsam redire, cum ad mortem ventum est, non ut tanquam anima humana, sed tanquam Deus ipse vivat. Et cap. 22. Rident, inquit, spem omnem, quam de resurrectione habemus, idque jam nobis evenisse dicunt, quod adhuc exspectamus.
english: IV. From the more recent who profess Christ's name, not indeed so many proceed to that temerity and profanity that they openly deny the resurrection of the flesh: yet there are not lacking those who are not ashamed to call back from hell the ancient heresies interpolated and crusted over even in this part of doctrine. Under the emperor, son of Ahenobarbus, Amalric the Paris doctor, having embraced this error among others, was burned at Paris with companions and followers. Pope John XXIII denied the resurrection of the flesh just as he denied the immortality of the soul.

Concerning the Libertines arisen in our fathers' memory, having many things in common with Cerdo, Valentinus, and Marcion, the great John Calvin (Instruction chapter 3): Whatever, he says, Christians hold concerning eternal life, concerning the resurrection, is a fable to them. For they imagine this — that the human soul, which is God, returns to itself when death has come, not so that it may live as a human soul but as God himself. And chapter 22: They laugh, he says, at every hope which we have concerning the resurrection, and say that what we still await has already happened to us.

source_text: Sub finem libri de praescriptionibus indicat, primis saeculis haereticos hunc fidei nostrae articulum impugnasse, Saturninum videlicet, Basilidem, Ophitas, Carpocratem, Cerinthum, Valentinum, Ptolomaeum, Secundum, Marcum, & Colarbasum, Cerdonem ejusque discipulum Marcionem Ponticum, Lucianum, Apellem. De singulis videas Epiphanium episcopum Cyprium, qui a Simone Mago haereticorum in N.T. Ecclesia parente & duce, resurrectionem negatam docet, sectasque ab ipso natas in hoc errore perstitisse. Cui adde Theodoretum lib. 1. haereticarum fabularum. Johannes Philoponus Grammaticus librum de resurrectione scripsit, in quo corporum resurrectionem tollit, & multa inconsiderate loquitur, sanctos etiam patres irridens, ut notat Photius. V. In summa, si historiam Ecclesiasticam evolvamus, & authores, qui de haeresibus ex instituto scripserunt, palam sit, priorum saeculorum haereticos ferme omnes carnis resurrectionem negavisse.
english: Toward the end of On Prescriptions he indicates that in the first ages heretics attacked this article of our faith — namely Saturninus, Basilides, the Ophites, Carpocrates, Cerinthus, Valentinus, Ptolemy, Secundus, Marcus, and Colarbasus, Cerdo and his disciple Marcion of Pontus, Lucian, Apelles. Concerning each see Epiphanius bishop of Cyprus, who teaches that from Simon Magus, parent and leader of the heretics in the New Testament Church, the resurrection was denied, and that the sects born from him persisted in this error. Add to him Theodoret (Heretical Fables book 1). Johannes Philoponus the Grammarian wrote a book On the Resurrection in which he takes away the resurrection of bodies and speaks many things inconsiderately, even mocking the holy fathers, as Photius notes.
V. In sum, if we unroll ecclesiastical history and the authors who wrote on heresies by design, it is plain that nearly all the heretics of the prior ages denied the resurrection of the flesh.

source_text: I. De Sadduceis constat ex historia Euangelica & Actis Apostolorum. Hymenaeus & Philetus dicebant resurrectionem jam esse factam 2.Tim. 2.18. quia existimabant, non aliam quam spiritualem, quae e peccatis per regenerationem est, promitti, ut Haymo & Lyranus explicant: vel quia resurrectionem in successione, quae per procreationem liberorum fit, constituebant, ut Theodoretus de illis tradit, deque Severi & Hermiae discipulis Augustinus haeres. 89. ad Quodvultdeum.
english: I. Concerning the Sadducees it is established from the Gospel history and the Acts of the Apostles. Hymenaeus and Philetus said that the resurrection had already happened (2 Timothy 2:18), because they judged that no other than a spiritual one — which is from sins through regeneration — is promised, as Haymo and Lyra explain: or because they set the resurrection in succession which happens through the procreation of children, as Theodoret hands down concerning them, and Augustine concerning the disciples of Severus and Hermias (Heresy 89 to Quodvultdeus).

source_text: II. Praeter hos quoque resurrectionem negasse Carpocratem, docet Augustinus haeres. 7. Marcum quendam, haeresi 14. Cainanos, haeresi 21. Severianos, haeresi 24. Hierarchitas, haeresi 47. Seleucianos & Proclianitas, haeresi 59. & 60. III. Irenaeus quoque libro 5. cap. 4. & seqq. contra Valentinianos sive Gnosticos scribens ait, eos salutem carnis exclusisse, negasse, regenerationem ejus sprevise, dicentes non eam capacem esse incorruptibilitatis & donationis Dei, quae est vita aeterna. IV. Tertullianus item libro de praescriptionibus docet cap. 15. a tota ista Gnosticorum colluvie negatam fuisse resurrectionem: Paulus, inquiens, notat negatores & dubitatores resurrectionis. Haec opinio propria Sadduceorum: partem ejus usurpat Marcion & Apelles & Valentinus. Cur autem partem dicat, rationem reddit cap. 16. nempe Sadduceos nec animae nec carnis admittere salutem, immortalitatem videlicet & restaurationem: at hi, qui Christianorum nomen jactitabant, eam quidem animae concesserunt, carni vero nequaquam. Unde etiam Tertullianus cap. 20. eos partiarios sententiae Sadduceorum appellavit.
english: II. Besides these Augustine also teaches that Carpocrates denied the resurrection (Heresy 7); a certain Marcus (Heresy 14); the Cainites (Heresy 21); the Severians (Heresy 24); the Hieracites (Heresy 47); the Seleucians and Proclianites (Heresies 59 and 60).

III. Irenaeus also, writing against the Valentinians or Gnostics (book 5, chapter 4 and following), says that they excluded the salvation of the flesh, denied it, despised its regeneration, saying that it is not capable of incorruptibility and of God's gift, which is eternal life.

IV. Tertullian likewise in On Prescriptions chapter 15 teaches that the resurrection was denied by that whole Gnostic bilge: Paul, he says, notes deniers and doubters of the resurrection. This opinion is proper to the Sadducees: Marcion and Apelles and Valentinus usurp part of it. But why he says part, he gives the reason in chapter 16 — namely that the Sadducees admit salvation neither of soul nor of flesh, namely immortality and restoration: but these who brandished the name of Christians conceded it indeed to the soul, but by no means to the flesh. Whence also Tertullian in chapter 20 called them partiarii of the Sadducees' sentence.
